issues.claim: was split into East Ham and West Ham in the 12th century
issues.problem: The split was earlier; the 12th century is only when the names East Ham and West Ham are in use.
issues.correct: A charter suggests the first division happened between 958 and 1037; the names East Ham and West Ham were applied to the parishes by the end of the 12th century (East Ham first recorded 1204).
issues.suggested_text: The land here lies between the Thames, the Lea and the Roding. It was recorded about a century before the Normans as Hamme, and by the 12th century it had been split into East Ham and West Ham.

issues.claim: The landing place was on the Thames, where Putney Bridge is today.
issues.problem: No source found placing Putta's landing place at the site of Putney Bridge. Checked the Wikipedia Putney article (only gives 'Puttan hythe', Putta's landing place).
issues.correct: Sources say only that the name means Putta's landing place (on the Thames); exact location not given.
issues.suggested_text: The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Putelei. The landing place was on the Thames.

issues.correct: The station is in the London Borough of Lewisham (St Johns); the site touches the Greenwich boundary, but the infobox gives Lewisham.

issues.claim: They owned land here in the 13th century
issues.problem: The family did not own the land; they bought the aldermanry (the right to govern) of the City ward.
issues.correct: The ward was purchased by the de Faringdon family in 1279 and its alderman then gave his name to it (Wikipedia credits Nicholas; other sources credit William).
issues.suggested_text: In 1279 the family bought the right to run this City ward, and their name passed to the ward, a street and the station. Farringdon was one of the first stations of the world's first underground railway, opened in 1863.

issues.problem: Wrong former name for the opening; the station was not called Finchley (Church End) from 1867.
issues.correct: Opened 22 August 1867 as Finchley and Hendon; renamed Finchley (Church End) on 1 February 1894; Finchley Central on 1 April 1940.
issues.suggested_text: The station opened in 1867 as Finchley and Hendon. It became Finchley (Church End) in 1894 and Finchley Central in 1940.

issues.claim: built in the 1820s as a turnpike
issues.problem: The road was only authorised in the 1820s; it was completed in 1835.
issues.correct: The Finchley Road Act was passed in 1826 and the turnpike road was completed in 1835.
issues.suggested_head: Named after the road to Finchley, built as a turnpike from 1826.

issues.claim: Finchley Road was built in the 1820s as a new road to Finchley.
issues.problem: The road was authorised in 1826 but completed in 1835.
issues.suggested_text: It comes from Old English frogga, frog, and healh, a nook. Finchley Road was built from 1826 as a new road to Finchley.

issues.claim: so a gate was put across it
issues.problem: The gate was not across the main road; it stood across the side road (today's Woodford Road) to stop cattle reaching the main road.
issues.correct: The gate was placed across the modern Woodford Road to stop cattle straying from Wanstead Flats (Epping Forest) onto the main Roman road; it was demolished in 1881.
issues.suggested_text: Cattle grazing in the forest could wander onto the main road to Romford, so a gate was put across today's Woodford Road. It was removed in 1881, but the name stayed.

issues.claim: Named after the Godyere family, who held land here in the 14th century.
issues.problem: Hedge missing, and 'held land' is not supported; sources speak of a resident.
issues.correct: Hidden London: the name 'probably derives from a 14th-century resident called Godyere'. Wikipedia: from a family named Godyere 'who lived in the area'.
issues.suggested_head: Probably named after the Godyere family, who lived here in the 14th century.

issues.correct: John Goldhawk held extensive estates in Fulham in the late 14th century.
issues.suggested_head: Probably named after John Goldhawk, a landowner in the 14th century.

issues.claim: Named after John Goodge, who developed the land from 1746.
issues.problem: John Goodge acquired the land (1718); it was his sons who developed it from about 1746.
issues.correct: John Goodge obtained Crab Tree Field by marriage in 1718; his sons Francis and William developed the land from around 1746.
issues.suggested_head: Named after John Goodge, who gained the land in 1718.
issues.suggested_text: Before the houses were built it was a meadow called Crab Tree Field. His sons built on it from about 1746. The station opened in 1907 as Tottenham Court Road and was renamed Goodge Street a year later.

issues.claim: The 2nd Duke of Portland owned the land from 1734.
issues.problem: 1734 is the year the 2nd Duke married the heiress Margaret Cavendish-Harley; the estate came to the family later by inheritance.
issues.correct: Margaret Cavendish-Harley, who married the 2nd Duke in 1734, inherited the estate, which then passed through successive Dukes as the Portland Estate.
issues.suggested_text: The land came to the Dukes when the 2nd Duke married its heiress in 1734. The station opened in 1863 as Portland Road.

issues.correct: Wikipedia infobox gives the London Borough of Hackney as local authority.

issues.claim: 'Haggerston' means the boundary stone of a man called Hærgod.
issues.problem: Wikipedia hedges: the name 'may derive' from Hærgod, either his farmstead or a boundary stone.
issues.correct: First recorded as Hergotestane in 1086; probably Hærgod's boundary stone.
issues.suggested_head: 'Haggerston' probably means the boundary stone of a man called Hærgod.

issues.claim: The station opened in 2010 on the new East London line.
issues.problem: Misleading: an earlier Haggerston station opened in 1867 (closed 1940); the present one reopened in 2010.
issues.correct: Haggerston station first opened in 1867 on the line to Broad Street; the current station opened in 2010 on the East London line extension.
issues.suggested_text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Hergotestane. A station first opened here in 1867; today's station opened in 2010.
